Discovery

Problem discovery

When to use it: Before you decide what to build, to learn how people handle a problem today and where it breaks down.

Who to interview: People who have dealt with the problem in the last few months, including people who are not your customers yet.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about the last time you ran into this problem. What was going on?
  2. What did you do about it at the time?
  3. What tools, people or workarounds did you use?
  4. What was the hardest part?
  5. How often does this come up for you?
  6. What does it cost you today, in time, money or something else?
  7. Have you looked for a better way? What did you find?
  8. Is there anything about this problem we haven't covered that matters to you?

Discovery

Jobs-to-be-done switch interview

When to use it: To understand what made someone start using a product like yours, and what they were trying to get done.

Who to interview: Customers who signed up or bought in the last 90 days, while the decision is still fresh.

8-question interview guide

  1. Take me back to when you first started looking for something like this. What was happening?
  2. What were you using before, and what was it like?
  3. What happened that made the old way no longer good enough?
  4. Where did you look, and what options did you consider?
  5. What almost stopped you from switching?
  6. Walk me through the day you decided. Who else was involved?
  7. What did you expect would be different afterwards?
  8. Looking back, what has actually changed since you started?

Discovery

Persona research

When to use it: When you need to know who your users are, how they work and what they care about, beyond demographics.

Who to interview: A spread of current users across roles, company sizes or usage levels.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about your role and what a normal week looks like.
  2. Which parts of your work take the most time?
  3. What are you measured on, or what does a good week look like for you?
  4. Walk me through the last time you used a product like ours. What were you trying to do?
  5. Who else do you work with on this?
  6. Where do you go when you need to learn something new for your work?
  7. What has frustrated you most about the tools you use for this?
  8. What would you want a new colleague to know about doing this job well?

Discovery

New market or segment exploration

When to use it: Before you enter a new industry, region or customer segment, to see how their needs differ from your current customers.

Who to interview: People in the new segment who do the job your product supports. You recruit them yourself.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about how your team handles this today.
  2. Walk me through the last time it went well, and the last time it didn't.
  3. What tools or services do you rely on for it?
  4. How did you choose them?
  5. What rules, constraints or approvals shape how you do this?
  6. What do people outside your industry tend to get wrong about it?
  7. If you had a free afternoon to improve one part of it, which part would you pick?
  8. Who else should I talk to, to understand this well?

Discovery

Startup idea validation

When to use it: When you have an idea and want evidence that the problem is real and worth solving, before writing code.

Who to interview: People who match the customer you have in mind. Do not pitch the idea during the interview.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about the last time you had to deal with this. What happened?
  2. What did you try first?
  3. What did that cost you, in time or money?
  4. How are you handling it today?
  5. What do you like and dislike about how you handle it now?
  6. Have you paid for anything to solve it? Tell me about that.
  7. Who else in your life or work deals with the same thing?
  8. What would need to be true for you to change how you handle it?

Discovery

Day-in-the-life workflow interview

When to use it: To map the steps, tools and handoffs around the job your product is part of.

Who to interview: Active users who do the workflow often, ideally at least weekly.

8-question interview guide

  1. Walk me through the last time you did this from start to finish.
  2. What starts it? What tells you it's time?
  3. What steps come next, and which tools do you use at each one?
  4. Where do you hand work to someone else, or wait on them?
  5. Which step takes the longest?
  6. Where do mistakes or rework usually happen?
  7. What do you do when something goes wrong?
  8. How do you know the work is finished and done well?

Onboarding

Onboarding experience

When to use it: In the first weeks after signup, to see where new users get stuck and what helps them succeed.

Who to interview: Users who signed up in the last 2 to 4 weeks, both active and inactive.

8-question interview guide

  1. What made you sign up when you did?
  2. What were you hoping to get done first?
  3. Walk me through your first session. What did you do?
  4. Where did you get stuck or unsure what to do next?
  5. What did you do when that happened?
  6. When did it first feel useful, if it has yet?
  7. What, if anything, did you need from someone else to get started?
  8. What would you tell a colleague who is about to start using it?

Onboarding

Signup drop-off (did not activate)

When to use it: When people sign up but never reach the first meaningful action.

Who to interview: People who signed up in the last 30 days and did not complete setup or a first key action.

8-question interview guide

  1. What was going on when you signed up?
  2. What were you hoping it would help with?
  3. Tell me about the first time you logged in. What happened?
  4. What got in the way, if anything?
  5. What else were you doing or using at the time?
  6. How are you handling that need now?
  7. What would have needed to happen for you to keep going?
  8. Is there anything else about that experience you'd like us to know?

Onboarding

New customer first 30 days

When to use it: About a month after purchase, to check whether early expectations were met.

Who to interview: Customers who paid or upgraded in the last 30 to 45 days.

8-question interview guide

  1. What did you expect when you bought?
  2. What have you used it for so far?
  3. Tell me about a moment when it worked the way you hoped.
  4. Tell me about a moment when it didn't.
  5. Who else on your team uses it, and how?
  6. What have you had to change in how you work?
  7. What questions do you still have?
  8. How would you describe it to someone who has never heard of it?

Churn and retention

Churn (cancelled customers)

When to use it: Soon after a customer cancels, to learn what changed and what would have kept them.

Who to interview: Customers who cancelled in the last 30 to 60 days.

8-question interview guide

  1. Think back to when you first started. What made you look for something like this?
  2. Walk me through the moment you decided to cancel.
  3. What had changed, compared with when you started?
  4. What almost made you stay?
  5. What do you use now, including a spreadsheet or nothing?
  6. What did it do well for you, even if it wasn't enough?
  7. Who else was involved in the decision?
  8. What, if anything, would have changed your mind, and when?
Run this in Frank Link to this template

Churn and retention

Declining usage (at-risk customers)

When to use it: When a customer's usage drops, before they cancel.

Who to interview: Customers whose usage fell noticeably over the last one to two months.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about how you used it when you first started.
  2. How has that changed recently?
  3. What has been going on in your work or team over the last few months?
  4. When was the last time you used it? What for?
  5. What do you do instead when you don't use it?
  6. What would make it more useful to you right now?
  7. Who else on your team still uses it?
  8. Is there anything about your experience you'd like us to know?

Churn and retention

Downgrade interview

When to use it: After a customer moves to a smaller plan, to learn what they stopped needing or valuing.

Who to interview: Customers who downgraded in the last 60 days.

8-question interview guide

  1. What was happening when you decided to change plans?
  2. Walk me through how you made the decision.
  3. What were you using on the larger plan?
  4. What did you decide you could do without?
  5. How have things gone since the change?
  6. What would the larger plan need to include for it to make sense again?
  7. Who else weighed in on the decision?
  8. What do you still rely on most?

Churn and retention

Win-back (returned customers)

When to use it: When a customer comes back after leaving, to learn what pulled them back.

Who to interview: Customers who cancelled and then returned in the last six months.

8-question interview guide

  1. What made you leave the first time?
  2. What did you use while you were away?
  3. How did that go?
  4. What happened that made you come back?
  5. What was coming back like?
  6. What has changed for you since you returned?
  7. What would make you leave again?
  8. What should we know about the time you were away?

Win-loss and sales

Win interview (closed-won)

When to use it: Within a few weeks of a closed deal, to learn why the buyer chose you.

Who to interview: Buyers and key evaluators from recently won deals.

8-question interview guide

  1. What was happening in your team that started the search?
  2. What options did you consider, including doing nothing?
  3. How did you narrow the list?
  4. What mattered most in the final decision?
  5. Where did we fall short during the evaluation?
  6. Who was involved, and what did each person care about?
  7. What nearly made you choose differently?
  8. What would you tell a peer who is evaluating the same options?
Run this in Frank Link to this template

Win-loss and sales

Loss interview (closed-lost)

When to use it: Within a few weeks of a lost deal, while the evaluation is still fresh.

Who to interview: Buyers and evaluators from recently lost deals, including those who chose to do nothing.

8-question interview guide

  1. What started the search?
  2. What options did you look at?
  3. Walk me through how the decision was made.
  4. What did the option you chose do better for you?
  5. Where did we fall short?
  6. What did you think of the sales and evaluation process?
  7. What would have needed to be different for us to win?
  8. How is the choice working out so far?

Win-loss and sales

Stalled deal or no decision

When to use it: When a deal goes quiet or ends with the buyer keeping the status quo.

Who to interview: Prospects whose evaluation stalled or ended without a purchase in the last 90 days.

8-question interview guide

  1. What prompted you to look at options in the first place?
  2. What happened to that need?
  3. Walk me through what happened after the evaluation started.
  4. What else was competing for attention or budget at the time?
  5. Who needed to agree, and where did it get stuck?
  6. How are you handling the need today?
  7. What would have to change for you to look again?
  8. Is there anything we could have done differently during the process?

Win-loss and sales

Switched from another tool

When to use it: When customers move to you from another product, to learn what pushed them away and what pulled them in.

Who to interview: Customers who replaced another tool with yours in the last six months.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about the tool you used before. How did you use it?
  2. When did you first start thinking about replacing it?
  3. What happened that made you act?
  4. What did you look for in a replacement?
  5. What was the move itself like?
  6. What do you miss about the old tool, if anything?
  7. What has been better, and what has been harder?
  8. What would you tell someone who is thinking about the same switch?

Pricing and purchase

Pricing and value perception

When to use it: Before changing prices, to understand how customers judge cost against value, from real decisions.

Who to interview: A mix of customers who bought, upgraded, downgraded or did not buy.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about the last time you decided to pay for a tool like this. What happened?
  2. What did you compare the price with?
  3. How did you decide it was worth it, or not?
  4. Who else had to approve the purchase?
  5. What part of the product would you find hardest to give up?
  6. Tell me about a time the cost came up after you bought.
  7. How do you explain the cost to others on your team?
  8. What would make the price feel easier to justify?

Pricing and purchase

Plan and packaging fit

When to use it: When you are deciding what goes in each plan, or customers seem to be on the wrong one.

Who to interview: Customers on each plan, plus people who looked at the pricing page and did not buy.

8-question interview guide

  1. How did you pick the plan you're on?
  2. What did you read or check before deciding?
  3. Which features do you use every week?
  4. Which ones have you never used?
  5. Tell me about a time you hit a limit on your plan. What did you do?
  6. What was confusing about the plans, if anything?
  7. Who uses your account, and for what?
  8. What would make you consider moving to a different plan?

Pricing and purchase

Post-purchase

When to use it: Shortly after someone buys, to learn what made them buy and what nearly stopped them.

Who to interview: Customers who purchased in the last two to four weeks.

8-question interview guide

  1. What were you looking for when you found us?
  2. How did you first hear about us?
  3. What else did you consider?
  4. What made you decide to buy when you did?
  5. What almost stopped you?
  6. What was the buying process like?
  7. What happened after you bought?
  8. What would you tell a friend about the experience so far?

Product and features

Feature validation (before you build)

When to use it: Before building a feature, to check that the problem behind the request is real and common.

Who to interview: Customers who asked for the feature, plus customers who work around the same problem.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about the last time you needed to do this.
  2. How did you do it?
  3. What was frustrating about that?
  4. How often does this come up?
  5. What have you tried to make it easier?
  6. What happens if it doesn't get done?
  7. Who else is affected when this goes wrong?
  8. What would a good outcome look like for you?

Product and features

Feature adoption

When to use it: After launching a feature that fewer people use than you expected.

Who to interview: Customers who could use the feature: some who tried it and some who have not.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me about the last time you did the task this feature is meant to help with.
  2. How did you do it?
  3. Have you come across the new feature? Where?
  4. If you tried it, what happened?
  5. What did you expect it to do?
  6. What made you keep using your old way, if you did?
  7. What would need to change for it to fit how you work?
  8. Who else on your team does this task, and how?

Product and features

Beta feedback

When to use it: During a beta, to learn how early users actually use the new product or feature.

Who to interview: Beta participants who have used it at least a few times.

8-question interview guide

  1. What did you hope to get from the beta?
  2. Walk me through the last time you used it.
  3. What worked the way you expected?
  4. Where did it surprise or confuse you?
  5. What did you do when something didn't work?
  6. How does it fit with the rest of your work?
  7. What would stop you from using it after the beta?
  8. What should we know before we release it more widely?

Product and features

Product-market fit

When to use it: To learn who gets the most value from your product, why, and what is missing.

Who to interview: Recent active users. Ask the Sean Ellis question in a short survey first, then interview a mix of answers.

8-question interview guide

  1. How would you feel if you could no longer use the product, and why?
  2. What is the main benefit you get from it?
  3. Tell me about the last time it made a real difference for you.
  4. What would you use instead if it disappeared?
  5. Who do you think would get the most out of it?
  6. How did you first find it?
  7. What would make it more useful to you?
  8. Have you recommended it to anyone? What did you say?

Satisfaction and loyalty

NPS detractor follow-up

When to use it: After an NPS or satisfaction survey, to understand low scores in the customer's own words.

Who to interview: Customers who gave a low score in the last survey.

8-question interview guide

  1. What was on your mind when you gave that score?
  2. Tell me about a recent experience that shaped it.
  3. What happened next?
  4. How did that affect your work?
  5. What have you done to work around it?
  6. What would a good experience have looked like?
  7. What do you still rely on us for?
  8. What would need to change for your score to be different next time?
Run this in Frank Link to this template

Satisfaction and loyalty

NPS promoter follow-up

When to use it: After an NPS or satisfaction survey, to learn what high scorers value and how they describe it.

Who to interview: Customers who gave a high score in the last survey.

8-question interview guide

  1. What was on your mind when you gave that score?
  2. Tell me about a recent time the product helped you.
  3. What would you lose if it went away?
  4. How do you describe it to colleagues?
  5. Who have you mentioned it to, and in what situation?
  6. What do you wish it did better?
  7. What did you use before?
  8. What would make you even more likely to recommend it?

Satisfaction and loyalty

Power user interview

When to use it: To learn how your most engaged customers use the product and what they would push it to do next.

Who to interview: Customers with the highest usage or the longest tenure.

8-question interview guide

  1. How did you get started with the product?
  2. Walk me through how you use it in a typical week.
  3. What do you do with it that you think most people don't?
  4. What have you built around it, such as templates, scripts or processes?
  5. Where does it slow you down?
  6. What have you taught other people about it?
  7. What do you use alongside it?
  8. What is the next thing you'd want to do with it?

Satisfaction and loyalty

Support experience follow-up

When to use it: After a support ticket or incident, to learn how the experience felt and what it cost the customer.

Who to interview: Customers who contacted support in the last 30 days, with resolved and unresolved tickets.

8-question interview guide

  1. Tell me what happened that made you contact us.
  2. What had you already tried before reaching out?
  3. Walk me through the experience of getting help.
  4. How long did it affect your work?
  5. What was the outcome?
  6. What did you expect from support?
  7. How did it change how you feel about the product?
  8. What should we do differently next time?

Marketing and positioning

Messaging and positioning

When to use it: Before rewriting your homepage or pitch, to hear how customers describe the problem and the product in their own words.

Who to interview: Recent customers who chose you over other options.

8-question interview guide

  1. How would you describe what we do to a colleague?
  2. What problem were you trying to solve when you found us?
  3. What words did you search for, or use, when you were looking?
  4. What did you think we were when you first saw our site?
  5. What made you believe it could work for you?
  6. What were you unsure about?
  7. What other options did you think of as similar?
  8. What would you call this kind of product?

Marketing and positioning

Buyer journey and channels

When to use it: To learn where buyers first heard about you and what they did between first touch and purchase.

Who to interview: Customers who bought in the last 90 days.

8-question interview guide

  1. When did you first hear about us? What were you doing at the time?
  2. What did you do next?
  3. Where did you go to learn more?
  4. Who did you talk to about it?
  5. What content or conversations helped you decide?
  6. How long did it take from first hearing about us to buying?
  7. What made you act when you did?
  8. Where do you usually discover new tools for your work?

How to use these templates

  • Pick one decision. Each template supports one question you need answered. If you need two answers, run two short studies.
  • Edit the wording. Replace "the product" and "this" with your product name and your customers' own words.
  • Keep it about real events. "Tell me about the last time" gets a story. "Would you use" gets a guess. Follow up with "What happened next?"
  • Talk to the right people. The "Who to interview" line is a starting point. You invite them yourself.
  • Check the time. 8 questions with follow-ups usually fit a short interview. Use the customer interview cost calculator with your own numbers to see the hours and cost for your study.

FAQ

Are these templates free to use?

Yes. Copy them, change them and use them in any tool or on a live call. No login needed.

Does Frank find people to interview?

No. Frank does not recruit participants. You share the interview link with people you already have.

Yes. Frank has a remote MCP server at https://api.hifrank.ai/mcp, included on every plan, including Free. Works with ChatGPT, Claude and Muse, plus other MCP clients that support remote servers with OAuth.
